claims.text: High-entropy transition-metal catalysts contain heterogeneous surface active sites with different local electronic structures.
A conventional phase-separated binary alloy has more uniform active sites than a disordered high-entropy alloy.
Synergistic interactions among dissimilar active sites produce a distribution of intermediate adsorption energies.
The adsorption-energy distribution optimizes reactant and intermediate binding without over-stabilizing adsorbates.
Optimized intermediate binding enhances catalytic activity and selectivity relative to more uniform conventional catalysts.
ORR and OER kinetics associated with O2/Li2O2 redox chemistry govern Li–O2 battery performance.
The reversibility of Li2O2 deposition and decomposition directly determines Li–O2 battery performance.
Catalytic activity depends substantially on adsorption and desorption of intermediates at surface active sites.
Intermediate adsorption can be modulated by changing the orbital occupancy of transition-metal active centers.
High-entropy-site heterogeneity creates varied d-band centers and orbital occupancies.
Some high-entropy-alloy sites stabilize LiO2 or Li2O2 intermediates while other sites prevent their over-binding.
The division of adsorption functions among heterogeneous sites improves reaction kinetics and selectivity across multistep oxygen-redox processes.
Under identical Li–O2 operating conditions, the high-entropy catalyst will have higher round-trip efficiency than the phase-separated binary alloy.
Under identical Li–O2 operating conditions, the high-entropy catalyst will show more reversible Li2O2 deposition and decomposition than the phase-separated binary alloy.
Under identical Li–O2 operating conditions, the high-entropy catalyst will show higher oxygen-redox selectivity than the phase-separated binary alloy.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when adsorption and desorption are critical in Li–O2 oxygen-redox reactions, but may not apply to other reactions or extreme temperatures.
Surface-area and morphology differences could confound attribution of performance to electronic heterogeneity.
Electronic heterogeneity is difficult to distinguish experimentally from an increase in the number of accessible active sites.
Failure of the high-entropy catalyst to produce any statistically significant improvement in activity, selectivity, or efficiency relative to the phase-separated alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
